title: Correlation is a tilted ellipse, and it decides how input uncertainty reaches the output
summary: Two uncertain inputs that move together are a tilted ellipse of possible values, and a Cholesky factor turns independent random numbers into exactly that cloud. A linear rule then says how much of the cloud's width reaches the output, Monte Carlo checks it with an error that shrinks only as one over the square root of the sample count, and Latin hypercube or Sobol designs place the same number of samples far more evenly than random draws.

media.alt: Three square panels of 64 points each in the unit square: random points with visible gaps and clumps, Latin hypercube points spread more evenly, and Sobol points almost on a regular lattice. Printed discrepancies are 0.0073, 0.0004 and 0.0002.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F8.4 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard probability and metrology. The figure is the design system's synthetic F8.4 render, so no project number is quoted. Every number in the steps and the worked example was computed for this page and checked by script.

read_the_figure.question: For the same number of samples, which design covers the input space more evenly, and how much does that matter for the answer?
read_the_figure.axes: Each panel is the unit square of two inputs, x1 across and x2 up, with the same number of points (64) in each. The printed discrepancy is a number that measures unevenness: smaller is more even.
look_at: Gaps and clumps. Random points leave empty patches and bunch up elsewhere; a good design has neither.
Look along each axis separately. Latin hypercube puts exactly one point in each of the 64 slabs of x1 and of x2; random points do not.
Sobol points form a pattern that fills every dyadic box exactly once when the count is a power of two.
The discrepancy values: here random 0.0073, Latin hypercube 0.0004, Sobol 0.0002 (synthetic demonstration).
read_the_figure.proves: It shows coverage of the input space, not accuracy of any particular output. A design that covers well tends to give a more reliable estimate of an average, but only a convergence test on the real model shows how reliable.
if_wrong: Panels with different numbers of points: the comparison is not fair.
Only two of many inputs shown: a design can look perfect in two dimensions and be poor in the other pairs, so check several pairs.
A power-of-two count not used for Sobol: balance properties are lost between those counts.
must_check: Same number of points in every panel.
Discrepancy or another coverage measure printed, with its definition.
Axis ranges identical and in scaled units (0 to 1).
Which pairs of inputs are shown, and whether Sobol sizes are powers of two.

terms.meaning: The average squared distance of a random number from its mean. Its square root is the standard deviation, the usual 'plus or minus'.
The average product of the two deviations from the means: positive if X and Y tend to be high together, negative if one is high when the other is low.
Covariance divided by both standard deviations, so it is a pure number between -1 and 1 that measures how close the points lie to a straight line.
The table of all variances (diagonal) and covariances (off-diagonal) of a set of random numbers.
The lower triangular matrix L with L times its transpose equal to the covariance matrix: a matrix square root that is easy to apply.
The row of slopes of the output with respect to each input; it says how a small input change moves the output.
Estimate an average by drawing random inputs, running the model on each and averaging the outputs.
Cut each input range into n equal slabs and place exactly one point in every slab of every input, pairing the slabs at random.
A deterministic low-discrepancy sequence built to fill the space evenly at every length; the standard quasi-random design.
A measure of how far a point set is from perfectly even coverage of the unit cube.

remember: $\rho=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)$ and $|\rho|\le 1$. It measures linear dependence only.
A Gaussian with correlation $\rho$ has elliptical contours, tilted toward the line of positive or negative correlation. For equal spreads the axes have variances $\sigma^2(1\pm\rho)$.
To sample $\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)$: factor $\Sigma=LL^{\mathsf T}$, draw independent standard normals $z$, return $\mu+Lz$.
Linear propagation: $\sigma_y^2\approx J\Sigma J^{\mathsf T}$. A positive correlation between inputs that act in the same direction adds to the output variance; opposite directions subtract.
Monte Carlo error falls as $1/\sqrt n$: four times the samples halve the error.
Latin hypercube guarantees one point per slab in each input; Sobol points fill space more evenly still and can converge faster for smooth models.

understand.title: Easy: the ellipse and what it says
understand.text: Plot many pairs of two inputs. If they are unrelated the cloud is a round or axis-aligned blob. If they move together the cloud is a tilted ellipse, long along the line where both are high or both low, narrow across it. The width across the tilt is how much freedom is left once you know one of them. Correlation near 1 is a thin needle, near 0 a blob.

understand.title: Medium: why the tilt matters for an output
understand.text: Take a power P = V times I, with both measured by the same unreliable meter. If the two errors lean the same way, the product's error is larger than if they were independent, because both push P up together. If they lean opposite ways the errors cancel. The linear rule adds the individual variances and a cross term proportional to the correlation, and that cross term is what the ellipse's tilt contributes. Ignoring a positive correlation underestimates the output uncertainty.

understand.title: Hard: where the linear rule stops working
understand.text: The rule replaces the function by its tangent line at the mean. That is accurate when the input spread is small compared with how fast the slope changes, and fails when the function bends within the cloud: for a ratio with large relative uncertainties the output distribution becomes skewed and its mean shifts, and the standard deviation from the rule is wrong. Atlas S27 example 2 shows such a failure. Monte Carlo has no such limit but pays in model runs, and its error stays $\sigma/\sqrt n$ no matter how many inputs there are.

understand.title: Hardest: why the evenly spread designs help, and where they do not
understand.text: A random sample has uneven clumps. Latin hypercube removes unevenness in each single input (one point per slab), which removes the part of the error that comes from a function's separate dependence on each input. It does not improve the rate for interacting inputs (in the check below the error still fell as $n^{-1/2}$, only with a smaller constant). Sobol points fill every dyadic box once when the number of points is a power of two, and for smooth functions the integration error falls nearly like $1/n$ instead of $1/\sqrt n$ (measured slope of about -1.4 for a smooth 4D test integrand in the check). The price: a Sobol set is deterministic, so the usual standard error needs several independent scrambled copies.

steps.title: Variance, covariance and correlation
steps.note: The bound is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the two deviations. rho = +1 or -1 means Y is an exact straight-line function of X. Atlas S26 example 5 draws a correlated pair as a tilted bell.

steps.title: The covariance matrix and the ellipse
steps.note: The contour of a Gaussian density at distance c is this ellipse. Its axes are the eigenvectors of Sigma and its semi-axes are c times the square roots of the eigenvalues. With equal spreads the eigenvalues are sigma squared times (1 + rho) and (1 - rho), checked symbolically; the long axis lies along the 45 degree line.

steps.title: Tilt angle of the ellipse
steps.note: theta is the angle of the long axis from the x-axis. Numerical check with sigma_X = 1.5, sigma_Y = 0.8, rho = 0.7: the formula gives 23.1 degrees and the eigenvector of the matrix points the same way.

steps.title: Cholesky sampling: independent numbers in, correlated numbers out
steps.note: The product L L transpose reproduces Sigma, verified symbolically. A sample of 500,000 points made this way gave a sample covariance of [[2.255, 0.841], [0.841, 0.640]] against the target [[2.25, 0.84], [0.84, 0.64]]. Geometrically z is a round cloud, L stretches and shears it into the ellipse.

steps.title: Linear propagation of uncertainty
steps.tex: y=f(x)\approx f(\mu)+J(x-\mu)\ \Rightarrow\ \sigma_y^2\approx J\Sigma J^{\mathsf T}=\sum_i\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\Big)^2\sigma_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,\rho_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j
steps.note: The tangent-line replacement is exact if f is linear and a good approximation if the inputs vary little. This is the propagation law of the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Atlas S27 examples 0 and 1 apply it to P = VI and to g from a pendulum.

steps.title: For a product the relative variances add, plus a correlation term
steps.note: The partial derivatives are I and V, so J Sigma J transpose divided by P squared gives this. In the worked example below the same inputs give 2.24 percent for rho = 0, 2.72 percent for rho = 0.6 and 1.00 percent for rho = -1; a Monte Carlo run of two million samples agreed with all three to within 0.1 percent.

steps.title: Monte Carlo and its 1 over root n error
steps.note: The samples are independent, so their variances add and the mean divides by n squared. For the 'pi from random points' estimator the standard deviation is 4 sqrt(p (1 - p)/n) with p = pi/4, about 1.642 over root n; repeated runs gave 0.162, 0.053 and 0.0164 at n = 100, 1000 and 10,000, matching it. Atlas S27 example 3 and S24 example 4 draw this.

steps.title: Latin hypercube: one point in every slab
steps.note: Every one-dimensional projection has exactly one point in each interval of width 1/n (checked: 64 points in 3D, all three projections had one point per bin). The random permutations couple the inputs without any pattern. This removes the error from each input's separate effect but leaves interaction effects to chance.

steps.title: Sobol points are a digital net
steps.tex: n=2^m\ \Rightarrow\ \text{each dyadic box }\Big[\tfrac{a}{2^{p}},\tfrac{a+1}{2^{p}}\Big)\times\Big[\tfrac{b}{2^{q}},\tfrac{b+1}{2^{q}}\Big),\ p+q=m,\ \text{holds exactly one point}
steps.note: Checked for the first two Sobol dimensions with 64 points: every one of the 7 families of dyadic boxes (width 1 over 2 to the p, p from 0 to 6) had exactly one point per box, also after random scrambling. This even filling is why the discrepancy in the figure is the smallest, and why the integration error of smooth functions can fall nearly like 1 over n (measured slope -1.4 on a smooth 4D test integrand, against -0.5 for random points).

worked.title: How uncertain is the power, and how many samples to check it?
worked.problem: A meter reads V = 10.0 V with standard uncertainty 0.10 V and I = 2.00 A with standard uncertainty 0.04 A. The two errors have correlation rho = 0.6 because the same calibration enters both. Find the standard uncertainty of P = VI by the linear rule, then say how many Monte Carlo samples are needed to estimate $\pi$ to within 0.01 as a one-standard-deviation error, as a reminder of the cost of the $1/\sqrt n$ law.

solution.text: Relative variance with the correlation term.
Take the root and scale by $P=20.0$ W.
For the Monte Carlo reminder: the estimator of $\pi$ has standard deviation $4\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ with $p=\pi/4$. Set it equal to 0.01.

worked.answer: P = 20.0 W with standard uncertainty 0.54 W (2.7 percent). Without the correlation it would be 0.45 W, so ignoring a positive correlation here understates the uncertainty by about 18 percent. A simulation with two million correlated samples gave 0.5436 W. And to know $\pi$ to 0.01 by random points takes about 27,000 samples; a repeat of that run with 26,960 samples gave a spread of 0.0099.

analyze.q: In the reference figure the Sobol panel looks almost like a regular grid with a twist. Why is that good for estimating an average, and what could go wrong if the model's output has a periodic dependence on an input?
analyze.hint: A pattern that is uniform in space can still line up with a periodic function.

analyze.q: Two inputs have a correlation of 0.9 in the data but the study sampled them independently. Which direction does the output uncertainty change if the inputs act in the same direction on the output? In the opposite direction?
analyze.hint: Use the sign of the cross term: derivative product times rho.

analyze.q: On a correlation matrix plot a pair has rho = 0.05 but a clear U-shaped scatter. Why does the matrix call them unrelated, and what does that mean for propagating their uncertainty with a covariance matrix?

evaluate.q: A team ran 200 random samples of an expensive model and quoted the mean to three digits. What would you ask before believing the third digit?
evaluate.hint: The standard error is sigma over root n; compare it with the third digit.

evaluate.q: Someone reports 'the Latin hypercube converges faster than Monte Carlo, so use it always.' When does that hold, when not, and what test would settle it for a given model?
evaluate.hint: Separable (additive) models gain a lot, interacting ones little; compare error against n for both on your model.

create: Design the figure for a study with 6 uncertain inputs of which two are strongly correlated: which plots (a correlation matrix, a pair of scatter panels, a prediction band) would you include and how would you show that the design covers the space?
Write a short procedure for deciding between linear propagation and Monte Carlo for a new model, with the test that tells you the linear rule is no longer safe.
Choose a sample size for a Sobol design and explain why it must be a power of two, and how you would still report a standard error.

checks.q: Why does a correlation of +1 give a thin line rather than an ellipse?
checks.hint: Look at the smaller eigenvalue, sigma squared times (1 - rho).
checks.answer: The covariance matrix then has a zero eigenvalue: $\sigma^2(1-\rho)=0$, so there is no spread across the line, only along it. The two variables are an exact straight-line function of each other, and the 'ellipse' has collapsed into a segment.

checks.q: Two inputs have standard deviations 1.5 and 0.8 and correlation 0.7. What is the Cholesky factor?
With rho = -1 between V and I the power's uncertainty in the example is 0.20 W, below either input's relative contribution alone. Why does it get small?
checks.hint: The cross term is negative and equal in size to the two relative terms together.
checks.answer: The relative variance is $(0.010-0.020)^2=10^{-4}$, so $\sigma_P/P=1$ percent and $\sigma_P=0.20$ W. A voltage error that is high by 1 percent comes with a current error that is low by 2 percent and these partly cancel in the product. It is smaller than the 0.447 W of the independent case, which shows how a negative correlation can reduce the output uncertainty.

checks.q: You need the mean of a model output with error 0.001, and a pilot of 100 random samples gave a standard deviation of 0.5. How many random samples would you need, and is it realistic if each run takes an hour?
checks.answer: $n=(0.5/0.001)^2=250{,}000$ runs, about 29 years of serial computing time at one hour per run, so brute-force Monte Carlo is not realistic. Options are a cheaper surrogate model, a Sobol design (which can converge faster for smooth outputs), or a linear propagation if the checks show that it is accurate.

checks.q: You have four uncertain inputs and a budget of 64 model runs. Which design do you choose and how do you report the uncertainty of the result?
checks.hint: 64 is a power of two; one run is not enough to estimate a standard error.
checks.answer: A scrambled Sobol design with n = 64: a power of two, so the balance property holds. A Sobol set is deterministic, so it has no ordinary standard error. If the budget can be split, run a few independent scramblings and use the spread between their means as the error estimate; the cost is fewer points per set, so decide from a pilot whether the better coverage of one large set is worth more. If only one set can be afforded, report the mean with a bootstrap interval and say plainly that the error is bounded by the discrepancy, not by a sampling standard error.
